title: Metabolic plasticity underlies ferroptosis resistance driven by mutant p53 in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive malignancy characterized by late diagnosis, rapid progression, and resistance to conventional therapies. Mutations in the tumor suppressor gene TP53 are prevalent in this cancer and have been associated with gain-of-function activities that promote tumor survival. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, represents a potential therapeutic vulnerability. However, the influence of mutant p53 on ferroptosis susceptibility remains poorly understood.
METHODS: We employed isogenic pancreatic cancer cell models, including CRISPR-Cas9-mediated TP53 Knockout (TP53-KO) and transient overexpression of common mutant TP53 variants, to examine ferroptosis sensitivity. Cell viability, reactive oxygen species accumulation, lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial integrity, and metabolic profiling were assessed following treatment with ferroptosis inducers. Transcriptional changes were analysed by RNA sequencing, and functional contributions of glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were evaluated using metabolic flux assays. Pharmacological reactivation of wild-type p53 was tested in combination with ferroptosis inducers in vitro and in orthotopic murine models.
RESULTS: Deletion of mutant TP53 sensitized pancreatic cancer cells to ferroptosis, accompanied by increased oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Mutant TP53 expression preserved mitochondrial integrity and sustained bioenergetic flexibility under ferroptotic stress. Transcriptomic analyses revealed a multi-layered adaptive program, including upregulation of antioxidant and metabolic genes, and activation of PI3K-AKT signaling, which is associated to a selective glycolytic shift to maintain ATP levels. Functional modulation confirmed that glucose supplementation enhanced, whereas glycolytic inhibition impaired, survival under ferroptotic conditions in mutant TP53-expressing cells, but not in TP53-KO cells. Pharmacological reactivation of wild-type p53 disrupted this adaptive network, abrogating glycolytic reprogramming and significantly increasing ferroptotic cell death both in vitro and in vivo.
CONCLUSIONS: Mutant p53 orchestrates transcriptional and metabolic plasticity that confers ferroptosis resistance in pancreatic cancer. Reactivating wild-type p53 in combination with ferroptosis induction overcomes this resistance, highlighting a therapeutically actionable vulnerability and supporting the development of combinatorial strategies for this aggressive malignancy.

title: Targeting CDC7 Overcomes Gemcitabine Resistance in Cholangiocarcinoma by Inducing Cellular Senescence.
abstract: Advanced-stage cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) frequently develops resistance to chemotherapy, highlighting an urgent unmet need for novel therapeutic strategies. Here, we analyzed 16 pairs of CCA and adjacent non-tumor tissues, and demonstrated that dysregulation of the cell cycle machinery is a hallmark of CCA, closely associated with chemoresistance and poor prognosis. Targeting aberrant cell cycle regulation therefore represents a promising approach to improve current treatment outcomes. We identify the CDC7 inhibitor XL413 as an effective agent capable of re-sensitizing gemcitabine-resistant tumors across multiple preclinical models of CCA. Mechanistic analyses, including transcriptomic profiling, reveal that combination therapy activates senescence-associated pathways, with therapeutic efficacy is mediated via a ROS-DNA damage-senescence cascade. Notably, synergistic induction of cellular senescence is observed in CCA cells upon co-treatment with a CDC7 inhibitor and gemcitabine. Collectively, these findings provide robust preclinical evidence supporting the combination of gemcitabine and CDC7 inhibitors as a viable therapeutic strategy to enhance the clinical management of CCA.

title: Systemic antitumor responses to hypofractionated radiotherapy plus Poly(I:C) in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma: A phase 2 trial.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The abscopal effect, regression of unirradiated tumors after localized radiotherapy, is rare. Whether hypofractionated radiotherapy (HFRT) plus the innate immune agonist polyinosinic-polycytidylic acid [Poly(I:C)] amplifies systemic antitumor immunity in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma is unclear.
METHODS: In this single-arm, phase 2 trial (ChiCTR2100053441), 37 patients received HFRT plus subcutaneous Poly(I:C); 33 were response evaluable. Outcomes were compared with 33 propensity score-matched patients treated with HFRT alone. The primary endpoint was the objective response rate per RECIST v.1.1; secondary endpoints included progression-free survival, overall survival, and safety; and abscopal response was prespecified. Mechanisms were explored by single-cell RNA sequencing and flow cytometry in patients and by CD8 depletion and CD28 blockade in mice.
FINDINGS: HFRT plus Poly(I:C) was well tolerated; it was associated with a higher objective response rate (54.5% vs. 21.2%; p = 0.011) and abscopal response rate (45.0% vs. 10.5%; p = 0.042) as well as longer progression-free survival (8.4 vs. 4.6 months; adjusted hazard ratio = 0.542; p = 0.042) and overall survival (not reached vs. 13.6 months; adjusted hazard ratio = 0.386; p = 0.011) vs. HFRT alone. The progression-free survival benefit was also higher in patients concurrently receiving tyrosine kinase inhibitors (p for interaction = 0.013). Peripheral CD8+CD28+ T cell expansion correlated with abscopal tumor control; in mice, CD8+ T cells and CD28 co-stimulation were required for this effect.
CONCLUSIONS: HFRT plus Poly(I:C) showed promising systemic antitumor activity with manageable safety in advanced hepatocellular carcinoma, with CD8+CD28+ T cells as an immune correlate of response. These exploratory findings warrant confirmation in randomized trials.

title: SRSF1-DLAT axis drives mitochondrial fusion to confer therapy resistance in diabetes-associated pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Patients with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and concurrent diabetes mellitus frequently exhibit poor outcomes. This study aims to elucidate the molecular mechanism linking diabetes with therapeutic failure.
METHODS: We integrated clinical analysis, diabetic-KPC mouse models, multi-omics approaches including scRNA-seq and eCLIP-seq analysis, and functional validations to investigate the mechanisms of therapy resistance in PDAC associated with diabetes.
RESULTS: It was found that pancreatic cancer with concurrent diabetes is prone to chemoresistance, which is accompanied by Serine/arginine-rich splicing factor 1(SRSF1)-driven altered splicing and expression of Dihydrolipoamide S-Acetyltransferase(DLAT). Our results showed that lactate accumulation in the diabetic tumor microenvironment induces K48-lactylation and stabilization of SRSF1. Crucially, stabilized SRSF1 directly binds to DLAT pre-mRNA, promoting the retention of Exon 5. This enhanced exon retention prevents nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) of DLAT, thereby elevating DLAT protein levels.The resulting SRSF1/DLAT axis drives mitochondrial hyperfusion, conferring chemoresistance by inhibiting senescence and apoptosis. Furthermore, the hyperfusion of mitochondria facilitates immune evasion by promoting the acetylation and stabilization of PD-L1. Notably, pharmacological intervention with Berberine effectively suppressed this SRSF1-DLAT axis, thereby re-sensitizing diabetes-associated PDAC tumors to combined chemo- and immunotherapy in vivo.
CONCLUSIONS: Our findings reveal that the SRSF1-DLAT-mitochondrial fusion axis drives therapeutic resistance in diabetes-associated PDAC. Targeting this metabolic-immune crosstalk offers a promising strategy for PDAC treatment.
journal: Drug resistance updates : reviews and commentaries in antimicrobial and anticancer chemotherapy

title: Epithelial-Mesenchymal Transition Is Associated With Perineural Invasion in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Perineural invasion (PNI) is a high-risk feature of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and is associated with aggressive behavior and poor outcomes. The biological programs associated with PNI in PDAC remain incompletely characterized.
METHODS: PDAC patients in The Cancer Genome Atlas were stratified by PNI status. Gene set enrichment analysis using Hallmark gene sets was performed to characterize transcriptomic differences between PNI-positive and PNI-negative tumors. Established immune, proliferative, and genomic annotations curated from prior The Cancer Genome Atlas analyses were used for downstream comparisons.
RESULTS: A total of 101 PNI-positive and 26 PNI-negative tumors were identified. PNI was associated with higher grade (P < 0.05). Gene set enrichment analysis demonstrated enrichment of multiple gene sets in PNI-positive tumors, including pathways related to cell proliferation (G2M checkpoint, mTORC1 signaling, E2F targets, MYC targets, and mitotic spindle), immune signaling (tumor necrosis factor-α signaling via NF-κB, interferon-α, and γ responses), and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT). Yet, no differences were observed in measures of tumor proliferation, aggressiveness, mutational burden, immune response, or immune cell infiltration within the tumor microenvironment. In contrast, EMT enrichment was supported by concordant biological features, including increased infiltration of mesenchymal cells and elevated expression of EMT-associated genes in PNI-positive tumors.
CONCLUSIONS: PNI-positive PDAC demonstrate enrichment of EMT-related transcriptional programs with concordant microenvironmental and gene-level support.

title: Oncogenic KRAS-MAPK signaling sustains a CD73 dependent therapeutic vulnerability in pancreatic cancer
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is predominantly driven by oncogenic KRAS signaling and sustained by a desmoplastic, immunosuppressive microenvironment limiting therapeutic response. CD73 mediated adenosine signaling supports this immune-excluded, tumor supportive microenvironment. Whether dual targeting of KRAS-MAPK and CD73 signaling creates a therapeutic opportunity to improve tumor control remains unexplored. Analysis of KRAS mutant cancer cell lines revealed increased expression of NT5E and adenosine receptor ADORA2B. Pharmacologic and genetic suppression of oncogenic KRAS inhibited CD73 expression through a MAPK-dependent program. In syngeneic KPC tumors, conversely, CD73 inhibition with quemliclustat increased ERK phosphorylation in vivo, suggesting adaptive MAPK activation following CD73 blockade. Combined CD73 and RAS(ON) inhibition in vivo produced the strongest antitumor response, reducing endpoint tumor volume beyond either monotherapy. This combination significantly suppressed tumor proliferation and SMA-positive stroma and resulted in a substantial reduction in CD163-positive macrophage infiltration. RAS-MAPK targeted therapy was also associated with increased CD8-positive T cell infiltration and granzyme B-positive staining. As therapeutic responses in PDAC have been linked to the gut microbiome, we further examined treatment-associated changes in the microbiome. RAS-MAPK inhibition produced the most pronounced microbial alterations, which correlated with tumor volume and immune markers. Together, these findings identify KRAS-MAPK driven CD73 signaling as a therapeutic vulnerability in PDAC and support combined CD73 and RAS(ON) inhibition as a strategy to suppress tumor growth, remodel stroma, and alleviate tumor-associated immune suppression.

title: Testis-Specific MAGEA3/6 Regulate Glycolysis to Promote Metabolic Flexibility and Reveal Therapeutic Vulnerabilities in Pancreatic Cancer Cells
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is an aggressive tumor characterized by metabolic plasticity that enables cancer cells to survive nutrient deprivation and therapeutic stress. Melanoma-associated antigens A3 and A6 (MAGEA3/6), members of the cancer-testis antigen family with a previously identified protective role in spermatogenesis during nutritional stress, have been implicated in cancer progression and metabolic regulation. However, their contribution to metabolic adaptation in pancreatic cancer remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the molecular mechanisms underlying MAGEA3/6-mediated resistance to glycolytic inhibition using complementary gain- and loss-of-function models, pharmacological inhibition of metabolic pathways, cellular metabolic assays, and integrated transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and lipidomic analyses. MAGEA3/6 expression enhanced resistance to 2-deoxy-D-glucose (2-DG), with MAGEA6-expressing MIA PaCa-2 cells exhibiting a greater than 2.5-fold increase in the half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50). Conversely, MAGEA3/6 depletion reduced clonogenic growth and migration and increased sensitivity to 2-DG. Resistance persisted despite pharmacological inhibition of mTORC1, the pentose phosphate pathway, or glutaminase, suggesting metabolic adaptations beyond these pathways. Unexpectedly, MAGEA6 expression was associated with increased rather than decreased AMPK1 protein abundance, contrasting with previously reported MAGEA3/6-mediated AMPK degradation and suggesting context-dependent regulation of this master regulator of cellular metabolism. MAGEA6 also reduced hexokinase HK1 and HK2 abundance while increasing several downstream glycolytic enzymes, revealing discordant regulation of glycolysis. Seahorse analyses and integrated multi-omics profiling identified extensive remodeling of mitochondrial metabolism, glutamine-aspartate metabolism, phospholipid composition, lipid storage, and redox homeostasis. Interestingly, despite enhanced resistance to glycolytic inhibition, MAGEA6-expressing cells exhibited increased sensitivity to hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress, revealing a potential metabolic vulnerability. Given that MAGEA3/6 are physiologically expressed primarily in the male germline during early spermatogenesis, a process highly sensitive to metabolic and oxidative stress, these findings also raise important questions about their physiological roles in protecting developing germ cells and maintaining metabolic and redox homeostasis. Together, our findings recognize MAGEA3/6 as regulators of metabolic plasticity in PDAC and highlight how understanding their molecular functions in both spermatogenesis and cancer may uncover previously unrecognized metabolic vulnerabilities and potential therapeutic opportunities.
